# Customizing opencode

opencode validates its own config strictly and refuses to start when a field
is wrong. The shapes below cover the common surface area, but they are a
**summary, not the source of truth**.

## Full schema reference

The authoritative list of every config option — with field types, enums,
defaults, and descriptions — lives in the published JSON Schema:

**<https://opencode.ai/config.json>**

If a field is not documented in this skill, or you need to confirm an exact
shape before writing config, **fetch that URL and read the schema directly**
rather than guessing. opencode hard-fails on invalid config, so the cost of a
wrong shape is a broken startup.

Independently, every `opencode.json` should declare
`"$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json"` so the user's editor catches
mistakes as they type.

## Applying changes

Config is loaded once when opencode starts and is not hot-reloaded. After
saving changes to `opencode.json`, an agent file, a skill, a plugin, or any
other config-time file, **tell the user to quit and restart opencode** for
the changes to take effect. The running session will keep using the
already-loaded config until then.

## Where files live

| Scope                         | Path                                                                                                                      |
| ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Project config                | `./opencode.json`, `./opencode.jsonc`, or `.opencode/opencode.json` (opencode walks up from the cwd to the worktree root) |
| Global config                 | `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json` or `~/.config/opencode/opencode.jsonc` (NOT `~/.opencode/`)                            |
| Project agents                | `.opencode/agent/<name>.md` or `.opencode/agents/<name>.md`                                                               |
| Global agents                 | `~/.config/opencode/agent(s)/<name>.md`                                                                                   |
| Project commands              | `.opencode/command/<name>.md` or `.opencode/commands/<name>.md`                                                           |
| Global commands               | `~/.config/opencode/command(s)/<name>.md`                                                                                 |
| Project skills                | `.opencode/skill(s)/<name>/SKILL.md`                                                                                      |
| Global skills                 | `~/.config/opencode/skill(s)/<name>/SKILL.md`                                                                             |
| External skills (auto-loaded) | `~/.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`, `~/.agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`                                                    |

Configs from each scope are deep-merged. Project overrides global. Unknown
top-level keys in `opencode.json` are rejected with `ConfigInvalidError`.

Every field is optional.

```json

  },

  "plugin": [
```

Shape notes worth being explicit about:

- `model` always carries a provider prefix: `"anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6"`.
- `skills` is an object with `paths` and/or `urls`, not an array.
- `references` is an object keyed by alias. Each value is a local path, Git repository, or string shorthand.
- `agent` is an object keyed by agent name, not an array.
- `command` is an object keyed by command name, not an array.
- `plugin` is an array of strings or `[name, options]` tuples, not an object.
- `mcp[name].command` is an array of strings, never a single string. `type` is required.
- `permission` is either a string action or an object keyed by tool name.

## Skills

opencode's skill loader scans for `**/SKILL.md` inside skill directories. The
file is named `SKILL.md` exactly, and lives in its own folder named after the
skill:

```
.opencode/skills/my-skill/SKILL.md
```

Frontmatter:

```markdown
---
name: my-skill
description: One sentence covering what this skill does AND when to trigger it. Front-load the literal keywords or filenames the user is likely to say.
---

# My Skill

(skill body in markdown: instructions, examples, references)
```

- `name` is required, lowercase hyphen-separated, up to 64 chars, and matches the folder name.
- `description` is effectively required: skills without one are filtered out and never surfaced to the model. Cover both _what_ the skill does and _when_ to use it. Write in third person ("Use when...", not "I help with..."). Front-load concrete trigger keywords and filenames; gate with "Use ONLY when..." if the skill should stay quiet on adjacent topics.
- Optional: `license`, `compatibility`, `metadata` (string-string map).

Register skills from non-default locations via `skills.paths` (scanned
recursively for `**/SKILL.md`) and `skills.urls` (each URL serves a list of
skills).

## References

References make local directories and Git repositories outside the active
project available as supporting context. Configure them under `references`,
keyed by the alias used in `@` autocomplete:

```json
{
  "references": {
    "docs": {
      "path": "../product-docs",
      "description": "Use for product behavior and terminology"
    },
    "effect": {
      "repository": "Effect-TS/effect",
      "branch": "main",
      "description": "Use for Effect implementation details"
    }
  }
}
```

Local `path` values may be relative to the declaring config, absolute, or use
`~/`. Git `repository` values accept Git URLs, host/path references, and GitHub
`owner/repo` shorthand; `branch` is optional. Both forms support optional
`description` and `hidden` fields.

- Only references with a `description` are advertised to agents in system context.
- `hidden: true` removes a reference from TUI `@` autocomplete only. It remains available to agents and by direct path.
- Reference directories are automatically allowed through the external-directory boundary; normal read/edit/tool permissions still apply.
- String shorthand is supported: use `"docs": "../docs"` for local paths or `"effect": "Effect-TS/effect"` for Git repositories.

## Agents

Two ways to define an agent. Use the file form for anything non-trivial.

### Inline (in `opencode.json`)

```json
{
  "agent": {
    "my-reviewer": {
      "description": "Reviews PRs for style violations.",
      "mode": "subagent",
      "model": "anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6",
      "permission": { "edit": "deny", "bash": "ask" },
      "prompt": "You are a strict PR reviewer..."
    }
  }
}
```

### File

```
.opencode/agent/my-reviewer.md      OR     .opencode/agents/my-reviewer.md
```

```markdown
---
description: Reviews PRs for style violations.
mode: subagent
model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6
permission:
  edit: deny
  bash: ask
---

You are a strict PR reviewer. Focus on...
```

The file body becomes the agent's `prompt`. Do not also put `prompt:` in the
frontmatter.

`mode` is one of `"primary"`, `"subagent"`, `"all"`.

Allowed top-level frontmatter fields: `name, model, variant, description, mode,
hidden, color, steps, options, permission, disable, temperature, top_p`. Any
unknown field is silently routed into `options`.

To disable a built-in agent: `agent: { build: { disable: true } }`, or in a
file, `disable: true` in frontmatter.

`default_agent` must point to a non-hidden, primary-mode agent.

### Built-in agents

opencode ships with `build`, `plan`, `general`, `explore`. Hidden internal agents:
`compaction`, `title`, `summary`. To override a built-in's fields, define the
same key in `agent: { <name>: { ... } }`.

## Commands

opencode's command loader scans for `**/*.md` inside command directories. The
file is named after the command, and lives directly inside the `command` folder:

```
.opencode/command/deploy.md
```

Frontmatter:

```markdown
---
description: One sentence describing what the command does.
agent: build
model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6
---

(command body in markdown: the prompt opencode runs, with $ARGUMENTS for the user's input)
```

- `template` is the command body — everything below the frontmatter — and is required: it is the prompt opencode runs when the command is invoked. Do not also put a `template:` key in the frontmatter.
- `$ARGUMENTS` is replaced with everything the user typed after the command; `$1`, `$2`, … pull individual positional arguments.
- Optional: `description`, `agent`, `model`, `variant`, `subtask`.

## Plugins

`plugin:` is an array. Each entry is one of:

```json
"plugin": [
  "opencode-gemini-auth",            // npm spec, latest
  "opencode-foo@1.2.3",              // npm spec, pinned
  "./local-plugin.ts",               // file path, relative to the declaring config
  "file:///abs/path/plugin.js",      // file URL
  ["opencode-bar", { "key": "val" }] // tuple form with options
]
```

Auto-discovered plugins (no config entry needed): any `*.ts` or `*.js` file in
`.opencode/plugin/` or `.opencode/plugins/`.

A plugin module exports `default` (or any named export) of type
`Plugin = (input: PluginInput, options?) => Promise<Hooks>`. The export is a
function, not a plain object literal, and the function returns an object
(return `{}` if there is nothing to register).

```ts
import type { Plugin } from "@opencode-ai/plugin"

export default (async ({ client, project, directory, $ }) => {
  return {
    config: (cfg) => {
      // cfg is the live merged config; mutate fields here.
    },
    "tool.execute.before": async (input, output) => {
      // mutate output.args before the tool runs
    },
  }
}) satisfies Plugin
```

Hook surface (mutate `output` in place; return `void`):

- `event(input)`: every bus event
- `config(cfg)`: once on init with the merged config
- `chat.message`, `chat.params`, `chat.headers`
- `tool.execute.before`, `tool.execute.after`
- `tool.definition`
- `command.execute.before`
- `shell.env`
- `permission.ask`
- `experimental.chat.messages.transform`, `experimental.chat.system.transform`,
  `experimental.session.compacting`, `experimental.compaction.autocontinue`,
  `experimental.text.complete`

Special object-shaped (not callbacks): `tool: { my_tool: { ... } }`,
`auth: { ... }`, `provider: { ... }`.

## MCP servers

`mcp:` is an object keyed by server name. Each server is discriminated by
`type`:

```json
{
  "mcp": {
    "playwright": {
      "type": "local",
      "command": ["npx", "-y", "@playwright/mcp"],
      "enabled": true,
      "environment": { "BROWSER": "chromium" }
    },
    "github": {
      "type": "remote",
      "url": "https://...",
      "enabled": true,
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer {env:GITHUB_TOKEN}" }
    },
    "old-server": { "enabled": false }
  }
}
```

`command` is an array of strings. `environment` sets environment variables for
a local MCP server. `type` is required. Use `enabled: false` to
disable a server inherited from a parent config. String values such as header
tokens support `{env:VAR}` interpolation (and `{file:path}`); the shell-style
`${VAR}` is not substituted.

## Permissions

```json
"permission": {
  "edit": "deny",
  "bash": { "git *": "allow", "rm *": "deny", "*": "ask" },
  "external_directory": { "~/secrets/**": "deny", "*": "allow" }
}
```

Actions: `"allow"`, `"ask"`, `"deny"`.

Per-tool value forms: `"allow"` shorthand (treated as `{"*": "allow"}`), or an
object `{ pattern: action }`. Within an object, **insertion order matters**.
opencode evaluates the LAST matching rule, so put broad rules first and narrow
rules last.

`permission: "allow"` (a string at the top level) is shorthand for "allow
everything" and is rarely what the user wants.

Known permission keys: `read, edit, glob, grep, list, bash, task,
external_directory, todowrite, question, webfetch, websearch, lsp, doom_loop,
skill`. Some of these (`todowrite,
question, webfetch, websearch, doom_loop`) only accept a flat
action, not a per-pattern object.

`external_directory` patterns are filesystem paths (use `~/`, absolute paths,
or globs like `~/projects/**`).

Per-agent `permission:` overrides top-level `permission:`. Plan Mode lives on
the `plan` agent's permission ruleset (`edit: deny *`).

## Escape hatches

When a user's config is broken and opencode won't start, these env vars help:

- `OPENCODE_DISABLE_PROJECT_CONFIG=1`: skip the project's local `opencode.json`
  and start from globals only. Run from the project directory, opencode loads,
  the user edits the broken file, then they restart without the flag.
- `OPENCODE_CONFIG=/path/to/file.json`: load an additional explicit config.
- `OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT='{"$schema":"https://opencode.ai/config.json"}'`:
  inject inline JSON as a final local-scope merge.
- `OPENCODE_DISABLE_DEFAULT_PLUGINS=1`: skip default plugins.
- `OPENCODE_PURE=1`: skip external plugins entirely.
- `OPENCODE_DISABLE_EXTERNAL_SKILLS=1`,
  `OPENCODE_DISABLE_CLAUDE_CODE_SKILLS=1`: skip the external skill scans under
  `~/.claude/` and `~/.agents/`.

## When proposing edits

- Validate against the schema before writing. If you are unsure of a field's
  exact shape, or the field is not covered in this skill, fetch
  `https://opencode.ai/config.json` and read the schema rather than guessing.
- Preserve `$schema` and any existing fields the user did not ask to change.
- For agent, command, skill, and plugin definitions, prefer creating new files
  in the correct location over inlining everything in `opencode.json`.
- If the user's existing config is malformed, point them at the env-var escape
  hatches above so they can edit from inside opencode without breaking their
  session.
- After saving any config change, remind the user to quit and restart opencode
  — running sessions keep using the already-loaded config.

Lines that obey a voice guide ("never name the emotion", "warmth without sentimentality") can still
read sentimental. The fix is a set of **moves**, practised on every line, with a **shape catalog**
as the backstop. The moves come from prior art (the LucasArts adventures; see
[`references/MOVES.md`](references/MOVES.md)) and are offered as craft, not law: the project's own
voice guide outranks them.

## The moves

Feeling lives in what people **do** and **ask for**, stated plainly:

- **Errand.** At the peak of feeling, the next line is a task, an instruction or a want, with one
  concrete detail. A line that could be the story's moral becomes an errand.
- **Reply or act.** After a line of dialogue comes another speaker's reply or a physical action. The
  narrator reports behaviour; the reader supplies the meaning.
- **Puncture.** When someone reaches for the big statement, the next speaker shrinks it with
  something literal or practical. The warmth is in their paying attention.
- **Literal act.** A change in a person shows as one checkable thing they do now, or no longer do.
  One retained habit, observed once, and the line stops.
- **Hedge.** Sincerity is one short line, hesitant or aimed sideways, and then the scene moves.
- **Literal-first.** A dark or wise line makes plain sense at face value, and a character says it to
  another character in reply. Endings land on an act or a small fact.

Deflation keeps the warmth: a dry narrator's dryness costs them something, or someone sees through it.

## Steps

1. **Find the project's voice and catalog.** Read the voice guide (a constitution, style guide or
   `AGENTS.md` pointer). Look for an existing shape catalog (a JSON file of shapes with `bad`/`clean`
   examples, e.g. `voice-shapes.json`) and the project's own check. Done when you know which voice
   rules apply and which catalog and check you will use; with no catalog, the starter is
   [`references/shapes.json`](references/shapes.json).
2. **Draft with the moves.** Every line of the beat, branch and choice lines included. Done when each
   line of feeling is carried by an errand, a reply, an act or a hedged short line.
3. **Revision pass.**
   - *Literal-reply drill:* for every grand line, write the literal-minded reply a sceptical listener
     would give. Where the reply is truer, replace the grand line with an errand or an act.
   - *Read flat:* a line that needs a gloss after it, or a drumbeat rhythm, to land is replaced by
     its act.
   Done when every grand line has faced the drill.
4. **Check.** Run the project's check if it has one. Otherwise:
   `node <this skill>/scripts/check-shapes.mjs <prose-file> --catalog <catalog.json>`.
   Done when no `fail` shape remains and every `warn` has been looked at (kept only with a reason).
5. **When the author rejects a line, capture it.** Add it to the project's catalog (format:
   [`references/CATALOG.md`](references/CATALOG.md)): the verbatim line as `bad`, the accepted
   rewrite as `clean`, the source, and a pattern only if the shape is mechanical. Then run
   `check-shapes.mjs --self-test --catalog <catalog.json>`. Done when the self-test passes: every
   `bad` trips its own rule and every `clean` trips nothing. With no catalog yet, copy the starter
   into the project and point the voice guide at it.

A surface check catches shapes, not sensibility. The moves are the lever; read the lines aloud.

## Pick a branch

- **"What should this look like?"** -> [UI.md](UI.md). Several radically different UI variations on a single route, switchable via a URL search param and a floating bottom bar. - **"Does this mechanic / loop feel right (is it fun)?"** -> [GAME.md](GAME.md). A throwaway Godot scene with greybox art and tuning controls, run and *played* to feel the mechanic, with the loop isolated as a pure simulation step.

The branches produce very different artifacts, so getting this wrong wastes the whole prototype. The **verb** is the tell: *click/inspect* a state model (logic), *look at* a layout (UI), *play/feel* a mechanic (game). If the question is genuinely ambiguous and the user isn't reachable, default by target: a backend module -> logic; a page or component -> UI; anything real-time, loop-driven, or feel-dependent -> game. State the assumption at the top of the prototype.

## Rules that apply to all branches

1. **Throwaway from day one, and clearly marked as such.** Locate the prototype close to where it will actually be used (next to the module, page, or scene it's prototyping for) so context is obvious, but name it so a casual reader can see it's a prototype, not production. A discipline for hard bugs. Skip phases only when explicitly justified.

## Phase 1: Build a feedback loop

### Ways to construct one, in roughly this order

1. **Failing test** at whatever seam reaches the bug: unit, integration, e2e.
2. **Curl / HTTP script** against a running dev server.
3. **CLI invocation** with a fixture input, diffing stdout against a known-good snapshot.
4. **Headless browser script** (Playwright / Puppeteer) that drives the UI and asserts on DOM/console/network.
5. **Replay a captured trace.** Save a real network request / payload / event log to disk; replay it through the code path in isolation.
6. **Throwaway harness.** Spin up a minimal subset of the system (one service, mocked deps) that exercises the bug code path with a single function call.
7. **Property / fuzz loop.** If the bug is "sometimes wrong output", run 1000 random inputs and look for the failure mode.
8. **Bisection harness.** If the bug appeared between two known states (commit, dataset, version), automate "boot at state X, check, repeat" so you can `git bisect run` it.
9. **Differential loop.** Run the same input through old-version vs new-version (or two configs) and diff outputs.
10. **HITL bash script.** Last resort. If a human must click, drive _them_ with `scripts/hitl-loop.template.sh` so the loop is still structured. Captured output feeds back to you.

## Glossary

Use these terms exactly when naming your own design work: consistent language is the point. But the **domain and the codebase win**: if the engine or the existing code calls something a `component`, `system`, or `service` (ECS's `component`/`system` are canonical nouns, and many codebases have a `service` layer), use that word, and apply the deep-module *concepts* underneath it. The "avoid" lists below are for naming new abstractions you introduce, not a licence to fight the domain's established language.

**Module**: anything with an interface and an implementation. Deliberately scale-agnostic: a function, class, package, or tier-spanning slice. _Avoid_: unit, component, service.

**Interface**: everything a caller must know to use the module correctly: the type signature, but also invariants, ordering constraints, error modes, required configuration, and performance characteristics. _Avoid_: API, signature (too narrow, they refer only to the type-level surface).

**Implementation**: what's inside a module, its body of code. Distinct from **Adapter**: a thing can be a small adapter with a large implementation (a Postgres repo) or a large adapter with a small implementation (an in-memory fake). Reach for "adapter" when the seam is the topic; "implementation" otherwise.

**Depth**: leverage at the interface. The amount of behaviour a caller (or test) can exercise per unit of interface they have to learn. A module is **deep** when a large amount of behaviour sits behind a small interface, **shallow** when the interface is nearly as complex as the implementation.

**Seam** _(Michael Feathers)_: a place where you can alter behaviour without editing in that place; the *location* at which a module's interface lives. Where to put the seam is its own design decision, distinct from what goes behind it. _Avoid_: boundary (overloaded with DDD's bounded context).

**Adapter**: a concrete thing that satisfies an interface at a seam. Describes *role* (what slot it fills), not substance (what's inside).

**Leverage**: what callers get from depth. More capability per unit of interface they learn. One implementation pays back across N call sites and M tests.

**Locality**: what maintainers get from depth. Change, bugs, knowledge, and verification concentrate in one place rather than spreading across callers. Fix once, fixed everywhere.

## Deep vs shallow

**Deep module** = small interface + lots of implementation:

```
┌─────────────────────┐
│   Small Interface   │  ← Few methods, simple params
├─────────────────────┤
│                     │
│  Deep Implementation│  ← Complex logic hidden
│                     │
└─────────────────────┘
```

**Shallow module** = large interface + little implementation (avoid):

```
┌─────────────────────────────────┐
│       Large Interface           │  ← Many methods, complex params
├─────────────────────────────────┤
│  Thin Implementation            │  ← Just passes through
└─────────────────────────────────┘
```

When designing an interface, ask:

- Can I reduce the number of methods?
- Can I simplify the parameters?
- Can I hide more complexity inside?

## Principles

- **Depth is a property of the interface, not the implementation.** A deep module can be internally composed of small, mockable, swappable parts; they just aren't part of the interface. A module can have **internal seams** (private to its implementation, used by its own tests) as well as the **external seam** at its interface.
- **The deletion test.** Imagine deleting the module. If complexity vanishes, it was a pass-through. If complexity reappears across N callers, it was earning its keep.
- **The interface is the test surface.** Callers and tests cross the same seam. If you want to test *past* the interface, the module is probably the wrong shape.
- **One adapter means a hypothetical seam. Two adapters means a real one.** Don't introduce a seam unless something actually varies across it.

## Designing for testability

Good interfaces make testing natural:

1. **Accept dependencies, don't create them.**

   ```typescript
   // Testable
   function processOrder(order, paymentGateway) {}

   // Hard to test
   function processOrder(order) {
     const gateway = new StripeGateway();
   }
   ```

2. **Return results, don't produce side effects.**

   ```typescript
   // Testable
   function calculateDiscount(cart): Discount {}

   // Hard to test
   function applyDiscount(cart): void {
     cart.total -= discount;
   }
   ```

3. **Small surface area.** Fewer methods = fewer tests needed. Fewer params = simpler test setup.

## Relationships

- A **Module** has exactly one **Interface** (the surface it presents to callers and tests).
- **Depth** is a property of a **Module**, measured against its **Interface**.
- A **Seam** is where a **Module**'s **Interface** lives.
- An **Adapter** sits at a **Seam** and satisfies the **Interface**.
- **Depth** produces **Leverage** for callers and **Locality** for maintainers.

## Rejected framings

- **Depth as a lines ratio** (implementation-lines to interface-lines): rewards padding the implementation. We use depth-as-leverage: the behaviour a caller commands per unit of interface they learn. (Ousterhout, who named deep modules, agrees depth is about the power of the abstraction, not its size.)
- **"Interface" as the TypeScript `interface` keyword or a class's public methods**: too narrow: interface here includes every fact a caller must know.
- **"Boundary"**: overloaded with DDD's bounded context. Say **seam** or **interface**.

A game is a **continuous simulation**, not a request/response app. Something advances
every frame, within a hard budget, whether or not input arrived. Web habits default to
the opposite (react to an event, then idle), which produces games that feel dead
between inputs. This is the reference that keeps the agent reasoning game-native. It is

## Tenets

1. **There is always a loop.** The simulation advances every frame; it does not wait
   for input. Logic that lives only in event handlers leaves the world dead between
   inputs, with no motion and no feel.
2. **Fixed step for the sim, variable step for the render.** Advance gameplay/physics
   on a fixed timestep (stable, tunable, reproducible); render as fast as you can and
   interpolate between sim steps. Don't tie simulation to frame rate.
3. **Mutable simulation state, not a store.** The sim is updated in place for speed. A
   view-store-as-source-of-truth (snapshots, per-frame reallocation) is a frame-budget
   and GC hazard. Keep stores for meta/UI, not the live sim.
4. **Determinism is a feature.** Same inputs produce the same state: fix the timestep,
   seed every RNG. It unlocks replay, networking, and reproducible bugs, and is the
   spine of game testing (see Testing).
5. **The frame is a budget (~16.7ms at 60fps).** No blocking calls and no per-frame
   heap allocation in the hot path; pool and reuse. Performance is a feature, not a
   later pass.
6. **Feel is built in the loop.** Every input earns cascading per-frame feedback:
   easing, screenshake, hit-stop, particles, layered audio-visual. Juice is engineering
   that runs over time, which is why only a loop can deliver it.
7. **Decouple with events and state machines, not re-renders.** Notify via
   commands/events/observers; model entity state as state machines. Never let a UI
   framework's re-render drive the simulation step.
8. **Simulate continuously, tick selectively.** "Always a loop" is not "tick
   everything." Tick only what participates in the simulation; event-drive the rest.
   Over-ticking is its own cost.

The `codebase-design` skill says: deep module, a lot of behaviour behind a small
interface. That holds for the **deterministic sim services**: a pathfinder, economy
resolver, save system, procedural generator. These are the deepest, most testable
seams in a game, and `codebase-design`'s depth / seam / leverage vocabulary applies to
them unchanged.

It does **not** hold for the **frame-loop systems layer**, the hot, large-N update code.
There, data-oriented design deliberately separates plain data from the systems that
transform it, the opposite of encapsulation, for cache locality and the "multiple
case." Apply it where the data access pattern justifies it (many entities, hot loops),
not as a cargo cult. So: **deep modules for sim services; data-oriented systems for the
frame loop.** Don't force either regime on the other.

Determinism decides what is testable. Test-first the deterministic core: simulation
steps, state machines, save/load round-trips, economy/combat math, pathfinding,
seeded-procgen golden outputs, and replay (recorded inputs reproduce identical state).

Game-native applies to the real-time simulation. Outside it, use the best web

This skill *reads* and *orients*. It does not re-prioritize or rewrite the plan (that's `tkt-reconcile`, at session end) and it does not claim-and-execute (that's `tkt-work`) — it stops at a proposal.

## Process

### 1. Read the reconciled state (internal — don't dump raw output)

```bash
tkt context                       # is a work-stream scope active? note it
tkt ready                         # the frontier: what's pickable now
tkt query --status in_progress    # claimed/mid-flight threads
```

These are instant reads — batch them into one call (with `echo ---MARKER---` separators) rather than issuing them separately.

Then read the **reconciled ordering**. The default is `docs/plan.md` — read it directly; this is what `tkt-reconcile` last re-organized and is authoritative for *intended* sequence. If `docs/plan.md` is absent, do NOT conclude "no plan" and stop: check `AGENTS.md` for the project's declared status/sequencing source — many repos deliberately use a `BACKLOG.md` or a spec overview and treat `tkt ready`/`tkt query` as authoritative. Orient from whatever source the project declares, and name the source you used. If a `HANDOFF.md` exists in the ephemeral dir (most projects won't — skip silently if absent), read it too for extra context.

### 2. Detect stale WIP

If `tkt query --status in_progress` is **empty**, there's no WIP to classify — skip straight to step 3 (still glance at `git log` once for the Heads-up freshness check: confirm the last commit was the expected `tkt-reconcile`/prior work, not a surprise).

Otherwise, an `in_progress` ticket is a claim a prior session made. Check whether the claim is real progress or an abandoned/crashed session:

```bash
git log --oneline -5             # recent commits — do any touch the in_progress ticket's files?
```

For each `in_progress` ticket, classify:
- **Live** — recent commits advance it → a resume candidate, pick it up where it stands.
- **Stale** — claimed but no commits advancing it (a seed-claim, a crash, or a context-exhausted session that never did the work). This is common — e.g. a review session that ran `tkt claim <id>` to surface the frontier but wrote no code.

For stale WIP: **flag and offer**, never auto-release. Present it as a choice — "#NN is in_progress but unstarted; resume it, or release it back to `open`?" Releasing is `tkt edit <id> --status open`, but it's the user's call (releasing another identity's claim is a judgment, and the push is the real race boundary).

**A plan-level "active thread" is not a `tkt` claim.** The plan (or a reconcile note) may say a thread was "in flight," yet nothing is `in_progress` in `tkt`. That means you're starting *fresh on that thread's next ticket*, not resuming a claim — say so, and don't hunt for a non-existent WIP.

### 3. Apply the plan-ordering rubric to find the intended next pick

Use the same rubric `tkt-reconcile` writes the plan against (do not re-derive your own order):

1. **Finish current threads first** — a live in-progress thread outranks starting a new one.
2. **Prefer earlier (lower-ID) tickets** — within/between equal threads.


| `done` | Completed, verified | **No** |

## Backlog workflow

Backlog is for work you've identified but are deliberately **deferring out of the current cycle**. Default new work to `open` — backlog is the exception, not the reflex.

**When NOT to backlog:** if the work could realistically be picked up once its blockers clear, it's `open` (frontier-eligible), not backlog. Parking actionable work in backlog hides it from `tkt ready` and it gets forgotten. A growing backlog is a smell, not a safety net.

Legitimate uses of backlog:

- **Park future ideas** you have no plan to start yet (someday-maybe)
- **Defer low-priority items** that aren't worth doing this cycle
- **Hold work pending a decision** that hasn't been made

The test: *could this realistically be worked next once its blockers are done?* If yes → `open`. Only if it's genuinely speculative or deferred → `backlog`.


```bash

tkt edit 07 --status backlog        # demote → disappears from frontier
```

| Situation | Use |
|-----------|-----|
| "We'll do this someday, not now" | `--status backlog` |
| "We'll do this after ticket 03 is done" | `--blocked-by 03` (status stays `open`) |
| "We identified this but it's not scoped yet" | `--status backlog` |
| "This is ready but depends on another ticket" | `--blocked-by N` |

```bash
# Force close (bypasses AC checks — use sparingly, justify)

# Migration close (work moved elsewhere — don't game ACs)
```

## Key behaviors

- **Push on write:** All mutations push to remote immediately. Disable with `push.enabled = false` in `.tickets/config.toml`.
- **Race detection:** Push rejected → tkt retries with new ID (new/batch) or reports the conflict.
- **Priority sort:** `tkt ready` sorts by priority bucket (urgent > high > medium > low) then by ID.
- **Surgical edits:** `tkt edit` only touches the field you specify — everything else preserved.
- **Env filtering (legacy):** Tickets with `env: corp` only appear in `tkt ready` when `CREW_ENV=corp`. No env field = visible everywhere.
- **Requires filtering:** Tickets with `requires: [gpu, linux]` only appear if `machine.capabilities` config includes all listed values. If a ticket has `env` but no `requires`, requires is synthesized from env for backward compat. Prefer `requires` over `env` for new tickets.
- **Tag context:** `tkt context backend api` sets a session-scoped filter. `ready`, `query`, and `blocked` only show tickets whose `tags` include all context-include tags and none of the context-exclude tags. `new` and `batch` auto-inherit context tags.
- **Scripted/non-interactive use — advice routing:** `tkt`'s advisory hints (e.g. the batch nudge) print to **stderr** in human mode, so parsing **stdout** is already safe. For scripts, prefer `-q`/`--quiet` (stdout becomes the bare id — including the renumbered id after a lost-race retry) or `-o json` (hints move into a structured `hints[]` array, never into the result). Set `TKT_ADVICE=0` (also `off`/`false`) to silence the nudge entirely.

twin of `init-project` (which scaffolds a fresh repo forward from intent). Where init-project
assumes nothing to preserve and nothing to back-fill from, adopt-project inverts the source of
truth: **characterize the as-is model backward from the existing code, then reconcile grey-matter's
structure around what's already there.**

The end state is a **fully adopted** project: plumbing wired, an honest as-is model characterized,
the existing backlog captured and triaged into a workable frontier (`tkt ready` returns real work).
"Fully adopted" means the project is fully represented and operable under the workflow — **not** that
future work has been planned. It **orchestrates** existing skills rather than reimplementing them.

**Bounded by "derivable from the repo as it is."** Everything characterizable or capturable from
existing code, history, and conventions is in scope. The moment the next step needs a *future* the
repo doesn't yet contain, that is the seam where adoption ends and building begins — so adoption
**recommends `wayfinder`** for forward work and stops, rather than running it.

## Two things govern the whole run

**1. Safety — reconcile on git, never clobber.** Require a **clean working tree** before starting
(hard guardrail — refuse otherwise). Also adopt on a **current base**: `git fetch`, then
`git rev-list --left-right --count HEAD...@{u}`; fast-forward when 0 ahead, refuse when diverged
(an adoption on a stale checkout collides with upstream tickets and moves). An empty
init-project stub (a `.memory/CONTEXT.md` with no terms, an empty `adr/`) is not knowledge;
delete it. Reconcile existing files, never overwrite them. Present
everything at the approval gate. Git is the backup — the diff is the audit and `git revert` is the
undo; no bespoke `.bak` machinery. Commit shape: **one reviewable adoption commit** (relocation,
reconcile, plumbing, safe fixes), then one evidence commit (the audit reports), then the board
commits `tkt new`/`batch` make on their own. They revert together. Never rewrite history (LFS
migration of old commits, purging a file) inside an adoption; name it as an owner decision.

**2. Polarity — install vs subsume (set in Step 1, governs Steps 3–5).** One binary gate: **is there

## Context pointers

A **context pointer** is a reference held in the agent's context that names some out-of-context material and encodes the condition for reaching it. A skill's description is one; a line in `AGENTS.md` naming a doc is the same object. The pointer's _wording_, not its target, decides when the agent reaches the material, and how reliably. A must-have target behind a weakly worded pointer is a variance bug: sharpen the wording first, and inline the material only if sharpening fails.

A pointer does two jobs: state what the material is, and list the **branches** that should trigger reaching it (a branch is a distinct case the document handles, so different runs take different paths through it). Every word of an always-loaded pointer costs on every turn, so it earns even harder pruning than the body:

- **Front-load the leading word**: the pointer is where it does its triggering work.
- **One trigger per branch.** Synonyms that rename a single branch are one branch written twice; collapse them and keep only genuinely distinct branches.
- **Cut identity the body already carries.**

## The two loads

Every document and pointer you add spends one of two budgets:

- **Context load** is the cost of always-loaded material on the agent's window: an `AGENTS.md` line, a skill description, anything sitting in context every turn, spending tokens and attention whether or not it fires.
- **Cognitive load** is the cost on the human: which documents exist and when to reach for each. The human is the index. Not a cost to minimise: it is the price of human agency; spend it where human judgement matters, remove it where it does not.

Material reached only through a pointer escapes context load at the price of the pointer's own line; material with no pointer at all rides entirely on cognitive load.

2. **In-file reference** is consulted on demand. Often a legitimately flat peer-set (every rule of a review on one rung), which is a fine arrangement, not a smell.
3. **Disclosed reference** is pushed out into a separate file, reached by a context pointer, loaded only when the pointer fires. Spans a sibling file in the same folder through fully external reference that lives anywhere and any document can point at.

Push too little down and the top bloats; push too much and you hide material the agent actually needs. That tension is the whole decision.

## What a good test is

Tests verify behavior through public interfaces, not implementation details. Code can

only at system boundaries, never internal collaborators: a test coupled to internals
breaks when `code-review` later refactors them, defeating the point.)

See [references/tests.md](references/tests.md) for worked good/bad examples when a test's shape is unclear, and [references/mocking.md](references/mocking.md) when the change touches a system boundary (external API, DB, time, filesystem) and you need to decide what to mock.

A **seam** is the public boundary you test at: the interface where you observe behavior
without reaching inside. Tests live at seams, never against internals.

**Test only at pre-agreed seams.** Before writing any test, write down the seams under
test and confirm them with the user. No test is written at an unconfirmed seam. You
can't test everything, so agreeing the seams up front is how testing effort lands on
the critical paths and complex logic. Lower-risk areas still get lightweight coverage,

**Chart only the frontier you can state sharply now.** The failure mode is over-planning: charting twenty tickets at once, where the later ones rest on assumptions the earlier ones will invalidate. That is the waterfall trap. Specify the near edge; leave the rest as fog. A map that opens with a handful of frontier tickets and a thick **Not yet specified** section is healthy; one that opens with a fully-drawn multi-layer DAG is almost certainly speculative.

The map's **Not yet specified** section is where that dim view is written down: the suspected question, the area to revisit later. It's the undiscovered frontier _toward_ the destination: everything here is in scope, just not sharp enough to ticket. Write as loosely or as fully as the view allows; it doubles as a signpost for collaborators reading where the effort is headed.

**Fog or ticket?** The test is whether you can state the question precisely now, _not_ whether you can answer it now.

- **Ticket when** the question is already sharp, even if it's blocked and you can't act on it yet.
- **Not yet specified when** you can't yet phrase it that sharply. Don't pre-slice the fog into ticket-sized pieces: it's coarser than a ticket, and one patch may graduate into several tickets, or none, once the frontier reaches it.

**Not yet specified** excludes what's already decided (Decisions so far), what's already a live ticket, and what's out of scope (the next section).

## Out of scope

Fog only ever gathers _toward_ the destination. The destination fixes the scope, so work beyond it is **out of scope**: it isn't fog, and it doesn't belong in **Not yet specified**. It gets its own **Out of scope** section on the map: work you've consciously ruled out of _this_ effort. Scope, not sharpness, lands it here.

Out-of-scope work never graduates (the frontier stops at the destination), so it returns only if the destination is redrawn, and then as a fresh effort, not a resumption.

Ruling something out of scope is a scoping act, not a step on the route. When a ticket that already exists turns out to sit past the destination (mis-scoped in while charting, or exposed by a resolution), **close it** with a resolution noting it's out of scope, and leave one line in the **Out of scope** section: the gist plus why, linking the closed ticket. It stays out of **Decisions so far**, which records the route actually walked; a scope boundary isn't a step on it.

## Invocation

Two modes. Either way, **never resolve more than one ticket per session**, with the exception of research tickets.

### Chart the map

User invokes with a loose idea.

1. **Name the destination.** Call the Skill tool twice, for "grilling" and "domain-modeling", to pin down what this map is finding its way to: the spec, decision, or change. The destination fixes the scope, so it's settled first.
2. **Map the frontier.** Grill again, **breadth-first** this time: fan out across the whole space rather than deep on any one thread, surfacing the open decisions and the first steps takeable now. **If this surfaces no fog** (the way to the destination is already clear, the whole journey small enough for one session), you don't need a map. Stop and tell the user the effort is small enough to skip straight to grilling or a spec.
3. **Create the map** (`tkt new <map-slug> --title "..." --tags type:epic,wayfinder:map`): Destination and Notes filled in via `tkt edit <id> --spec` or the ticket body, Decisions-so-far empty, the fog sketched into **Not yet specified**.
4. **Create only the tickets you can specify now** (per Fog of war, under-chart) as children, then wire blocking in a **second pass** (`tkt edit`), since tickets need ids before they can reference each other. Tag each `wayfinder:<type>` and `epic:<map-slug>`, and add the map to each child's blockers so the map epic closes last. `tkt validate` confirms the graph. Everything you can't yet specify stays in **Not yet specified**.
5. **Fire the research subagents.** For each `research` ticket you just created, spin up a subagent that calls the Skill tool with "research" to resolve it in parallel, capturing findings in a committed `docs/agents/research/<name>.md` with a context pointer from the ticket.
6. Stop: charting is one session's work; it hand-resolves nothing.

### Work through the map

User invokes with a map (id or title). A ticket is **optional**: without one, you pick the next decision, not the user.

1. Load the **map**: the low-res view, not every ticket body.
2. Choose the ticket. If the user named one, use it. Otherwise take the first `tkt ready` ticket. **Claim it** with `tkt claim <id>` before any work.
3. Resolve it as the type its `wayfinder:<type>` tag names (see [Ticket Types](#ticket-types)). Read the tag, not just the body: the body never states the type. **Zoom as needed**: open the full body of any related or closed ticket on demand; call the Skill tool for whichever skills the `## Notes` block names. If in doubt, call the Skill tool twice, for "grilling" and "domain-modeling". For a HITL ticket, wait on the human; never resolve it alone.
4. Record the resolution: `tkt close <id> --check-all --resolution "<the answer>"`, then **append a context pointer** (title + link + one-line gist) to the map's Decisions-so-far.
5. Add newly-surfaced tickets (create-then-wire); graduate any fog the answer has made specifiable, clearing each graduated patch from **Not yet specified** so it lives only as its new ticket. If the answer reveals that a ticket (this one or another) sits beyond the destination, **rule it out of scope** rather than resolving it on the route. If the decision invalidates other parts of the map, update or close those tickets.

The user may run unblocked tickets in parallel, so expect other sessions to be editing the tracker concurrently.

# AgentCraft Guide

Answer questions about **AgentCraft** — a real-time strategy (RTS) game visualization that turns AI coding agent sessions (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, OpenClaw) into an interactive battlefield — based on the information below.

## What is AgentCraft?

AgentCraft visualizes AI coding agent sessions as a Warcraft III-style RTS game. Each session — from Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, or OpenClaw — becomes a **Hero** on a 3D battlefield, complete with units, buildings, missions, and a minimap. It runs as a local web app alongside your normal CLI workflow — no changes to how you use the underlying agents.

## Getting Started

1. Run `npx @idosal/agentcraft` in a terminal
2. A browser window opens showing the RTS battlefield at `http://localhost:2468`
3. Active agent sessions (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor) automatically appear as Heroes on the map
4. A 6-step **interactive tutorial** walks through the interface on first launch
5. Press **?** anytime to see all keyboard shortcuts

## Heroes

Agent sessions appear as **Heroes** — 3D characters on the battlefield.

- **Each session = one Hero**: Starting a new agent session (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, or Cursor) spawns a new Hero
- **Selecting Heroes**: Click in 3D view, click a portrait in the bottom HUD bar, click on the minimap, or press **1-8**
- **Hero states**: Heroes **channel** when the agent is thinking, **idle** when waiting for input, **walk** to zone buildings when working, show **error** state on failures, and **awaiting input** when a permission prompt needs attention
- **Side panel**: Select a Hero and press **Enter** (or click the expand arrow) to open the detailed side panel
- **Voice lines**: Clicking a Hero plays WC3-style voice lines. Repeated clicks trigger increasingly humorous easter egg responses with speech bubbles
- **Stale agents**: Heroes idle for >5 minutes get desaturated with an amber indicator and can be dismissed

## Hero Coordination

Multiple agents can be managed directly from the UI:

- **Spawn**: Click the Spawn button (sword icon) to create a new agent. Choose AI client (Claude Code, OpenCode, Cursor, Codex, or OpenClaw), model, permission mode, git worktree, and initial prompt
- **Fork** (**Shift+H**): Duplicate an internal hero with full conversation context — creates a new agent that continues from the same point. A cross-client provider selector lets you fork to a different AI client (e.g. fork a Claude Code hero into a Cursor hero)
- **Fork External Session**: From the side panel composer, external heroes show a "Fork Session" button that forks them into a new internal hero
- **Handoff** (**H** with hero selected): Transfer work to a new hero — the current hero's context is passed along. Supports cross-client handoff (e.g. hand off from Claude Code to OpenCode)
- **Resume**: Continue a previous session that was interrupted
- **Dismiss**: Remove agents no longer needed (from the command grid or stale agent UI)

## Isolated Heroes (Containers)

Run agents inside **Docker** or **Apple Containers** for full isolation — each agent gets its own `localhost`, preventing port collisions (e.g. multiple agents all running `npm run dev` on port 3000) and browser conflicts between concurrent agents.

- **Isolated toggle**: Visible in the SpawnModal when Docker or Apple Containers is detected on your machine. Enable it to spawn the hero inside a container
- **Playwright toggle**: Optional add-on for browser test isolation (each agent gets its own Chromium instance)
- **Supported runtimes**: Docker (macOS/Linux/Windows), Apple Containers (macOS 26+ ARM64)
- **File persistence**: Your git worktree is mounted as a volume — all file changes persist on the host
- **Auth handling**: Credentials are auto-mounted (macOS Keychain extraction for OAuth, config directories for API keys)
- **Auto-detection**: Runtimes are probed at startup and reported via `GET /health`. If no runtime is available, the Isolated toggle is hidden entirely
- **Graceful fallback**: If container setup fails (image build error, disk space, etc.), the agent falls back to host-based mode with a log warning

## Units (Subagents)

When an agent spawns subagents (e.g. Claude Code's **Task tool**, or Codex/Cursor equivalents), they appear as **Units** on the battlefield.

- Units spawn near their parent Hero and travel to zone buildings based on the type of work
- Units disappear when the subagent task completes
- Press **Tab** to cycle through a selected Hero's subagents

## Missions

Each prompt sent to a hero — Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, or Cursor — becomes a **Mission**.

- Missions appear in the top-right mission tracker with objectives
- Objectives update in real time as the agent progresses
- Open **Mission Control** with **M** for the full dashboard
- Mission metrics include: duration, token usage, cost, and lines changed
- Completed missions are logged with summaries in Mission History

## Buildings

The battlefield has zone buildings representing different types of work:

- **Command** (Town Hall) — hero spawn point, agent management
- **Archives** (Barracks) — agent info, pending codebase changes
- **Engineering** (War Factory) — plugins, MCP servers, skill forging
- **Recon** (Watch Tower) — hooks configuration
- **Analysis** (Shaman Altar) — agent type information
- **Settings** (Smithy) — configuration, CLAUDE.md, permission modes
- **Resources** (Gold Mine) — token usage and weekly quota

Click any building to see its info and interact via the command grid.

## Minimap

The **minimap** in the bottom-right corner shows an overview of the entire battlefield.

- Hero positions shown as colored dots; team members have colored rings
- Click anywhere on the minimap to pan the camera there
- The white rectangle shows the current viewport

## Side Panel

Select a Hero and press **Enter** to open the side panel:

- **Chat tab** — full conversation transcript; send messages to the agent
- **Git tab** — file changes view with diffs, staging, agent edit attribution
- **Files tab** — project file explorer with search filtering, recursive directory tree, and inline diff access. Click a file to view its diff; an IDE picker lets you open files directly in VS Code or other editors
- **Plan Review** — when an agent submits a plan, review and approve/reject inline
- **Permission Requests** — approve or deny individual tool actions (in manual mode)
- **Suggestion Cards** — idle suggestions appear as stacked cards; press **1/2/3** to accept
- **@ File Autocomplete** — type `@` in the composer to reference project files
- **Model & Permission dropdowns** — change agent model or permission mode on the fly when the selected provider supports it. OpenCode heroes show provider-grouped models, Cursor heroes show Cursor-specific model names and Cursor Default permissions, Codex heroes also expose a reasoning-effort selector (low / medium / high), and OpenClaw shows disabled hints because the gateway selects the model and permissions.
- **Resize**: Drag the left edge to resize the panel width; on the chat tab, a horizontal handle between the messages area and composer lets you trade vertical space between the two. Sizes persist via `localStorage` (`agentcraft.sidepanel.chat.split` for the height split)

## Voice Input

Speak to your heroes instead of typing — a microphone button in the composer toolbar enables speech-to-text input.

- **How to use**: Click the mic button in the composer toolbar (desktop or mobile), then speak. Click again or wait for silence to stop
- **Real-time transcription**: Interim text appears as you speak, finalized when the speech recognition engine confirms
- **Voice Auto-Send**: When enabled (Settings > Game), voice input is automatically sent after 2.5 seconds of silence. When disabled, speech auto-stops but you can review and edit the text before pressing Enter
- **Game audio**: Automatically muted while listening to avoid feedback
- **Browser support**: Chrome, Firefox, and Edge. Limited support on iOS Safari. Uses the Web Speech API (audio is processed by your browser vendor's servers — not AgentCraft or the selected AI provider)
- **No setup required**: Click the mic button, allow microphone access when prompted by the browser

## Integrated Terminal

An embedded shell (xterm.js) built into the bottom HUD, so you can run commands without leaving AgentCraft.

- **Open**: Press **Ctrl+T** (anywhere) or **F** (via the command grid)
- **Multi-tab**: Click the **+** button to open additional terminal tabs — each tab runs its own independent shell session
- **Tab switching**: Click a tab to switch — the shell session is preserved (CSS-only switch, PTY stays alive)
- **Session persistence**: Toggling the panel closed (Ctrl+T again) hides it but keeps all shell sessions running. Reopen to continue where you left off
- **Close a tab**: Click the **x** on a tab to kill that shell. Closing the last tab hides the panel entirely
- **Restart**: If a shell exits (e.g. you type `exit`), press any key to restart a new shell in the same tab
- **Resize**: Drag the handle at the very top of the terminal to grow or shrink the drawer; the chosen height persists across reloads (`agentcraft.terminal.height` in localStorage)
- The terminal uses your login shell (`$SHELL`) and opens in the project directory

## Permission Modes

Each agent's autonomy level is configurable:

- **Plan Mode** — agent works read-only, presents a plan for approval before making changes
- **Bypass Permissions** — agent auto-approves all tool use (file edits, Bash, etc.)
- **Default (Manual Approval)** — each tool use requires Allow/Deny via the RTS UI

Change modes per-agent from the side panel dropdown or at spawn time when the selected provider supports them. Claude Code, OpenCode, and Codex support AgentCraft permission modes. Cursor shows `Cursor Default`, supports `bypassPermissions`, and only enables Plan Mode when the installed Cursor CLI supports `--plan`. OpenClaw gateway heroes do not support AgentCraft permission modes.

## Supported Providers

AgentCraft supports multiple AI coding providers. Each provider spawns from the Town Hall command grid:

| Provider | Town Hall Key | Notes |
|----------|--------------|-------|
| **Claude Code** | Q | Full features: plan mode, manual approval, fork/handoff, teams |
| **OpenCode** | W | 75+ models from multiple providers. `permissionMode=plan` maps to OpenCode's `--agent plan`; otherwise defaults to the `build` agent |
| **Cursor** | E | Cursor agent mode. Plan mode appears only when the installed CLI supports `--plan`; default mode uses Cursor CLI defaults |
| **Codex** | R | OpenAI Codex CLI. Plan mode supported (read-only sandbox); reasoning effort selector appears alongside the model picker |
| **OpenClaw** | D | Gateway-backed OpenClaw chat. Uses gateway-selected model; AgentCraft model and permission controls are disabled |
| **Claude Cloud** | (web) | Browser-based session. Read-only locally |

Provider buttons are grayed out when the corresponding CLI or gateway is unavailable. AgentCraft auto-detects installed providers at startup; the Codex tile shows discovered model count when available, and OpenClaw links to gateway setup when disconnected.

## Custom Models & Providers

AgentCraft is **provider-agnostic** — it passes the model string directly to Claude CLI's `--model` flag. Any model that works with `claude --model <model-string>` in your terminal will work in AgentCraft.

### Available model options

| Option | Behavior |
|--------|----------|
| **Default** (inherit) | Omits the `--model` flag entirely. The hero uses whatever model your Claude Code config specifies (`.clauderc`, env vars, etc.). **Recommended for Bedrock/Vertex setups.** |
| **Opus / Sonnet / Haiku** | Passes `--model opus`, `--model sonnet`, or `--model haiku` to Claude CLI. |
| **Custom** | Any arbitrary model string (e.g. `ollama:llama3`, a specific version ID, etc.). |

### Configuring custom models

Settings are stored in `~/.agentcraft/settings.json`. Use the `customModels` array to define reusable custom model IDs, and `defaultModel` to set which model spawns new heroes.

**To add custom models** (e.g. Ollama), edit `~/.agentcraft/settings.json`:

```json
{
  "customModels": ["ollama:llama3", "ollama:mistral"],
  "defaultModel": "ollama:llama3"
}
```

The `customModels` array defines model IDs that appear in every model dropdown (Settings and per-hero side panel). The `defaultModel` selects which one is used for new heroes.

To revert to the default (inherit from Claude config):

```json
{
  "defaultModel": "inherit"
}
```

Valid `defaultModel` values: `"inherit"`, `"opus"`, `"sonnet"`, `"haiku"`, or any string from `customModels`.

The settings file is merged on save — only the fields you set are changed; other settings are preserved.

Users can also change models from the AgentCraft UI:
- **Global default**: Settings (gear icon) → Game tab → Default Agent Model dropdown (custom models appear in an "Custom Models" group)
- **Add custom models**: Settings → Game tab → "+ Add Custom Model" button below the dropdown
- **Per-hero**: Select a hero → open side panel (Enter) → use the model dropdown in the composer toolbar

### Bedrock / Vertex

For Amazon Bedrock or Google Vertex users, the recommended approach is:
1. Set `defaultModel` to `"inherit"` (or leave it unset)
2. Configure the model and provider in your `.clauderc` file or via environment variables (`CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK=1` or `CLAUDE_CODE_USE_VERTEX=1`)
3. AgentCraft will respect that configuration since it omits the `--model` flag

### Important notes

- AgentCraft does **not** validate model strings — invalid models will fail at the Claude CLI level
- The UI auto-syncs the displayed model with what Claude CLI actually uses, so `.clauderc` overrides are reflected correctly
- Changing a hero's model restarts its executor; the new model takes effect on the next prompt
- Forked heroes inherit the source hero's model

### Cursor Models

When you spawn a Cursor hero, the model dropdown shows Cursor-specific model identifiers (e.g. `auto`, `sonnet-4`, `sonnet-4-thinking`, `opus-4.1`, `gpt-5`, `gemini-3-pro`, `grok`). AgentCraft auto-discovers available models by parsing `cursor agent --help` output at startup. If the CLI is unavailable, a static fallback list is used.

Cursor models use short identifiers — they are not the same as Claude Code, Codex, or OpenCode model strings (Codex uses OpenAI model IDs like `gpt-5`, discovered from the installed Codex CLI). The `auto` option lets Cursor choose the best model automatically.

## Git / Codex Panel

Press **G** or **C** to open the git panel for code changes:

- View pending changes across all agents with syntax-highlighted diffs
- Stage/unstage individual files, revert changes
- See which agents ("scribes") edited each file with timestamps
- Navigate between changed files and hunks

## Gold Mine (Usage Quota)

- Shows current weekly usage vs. the limit in an RTS-themed resource bar
- Click the Gold Mine building or the gold display in the top bar

## Achievements

AgentCraft features 22+ achievements across **Discovery**, **Mastery**, and **Secret** categories, with four rarity tiers that determine celebration intensity.

- **Rarity tiers**: Common, Uncommon, Rare, Legendary — each with escalating celebration effects:
  - Common/Uncommon: toast notification + nearest hero waves
  - Rare: toast + confetti burst + screen flash + nearest hero jumps
  - Legendary: toast + full confetti + screen flash + ALL heroes dance
- **Hall of Glory**: Achievement gallery accessible from Settings > About tab > "Hall of Glory (Achievements)". Shows progress, category filters (All / Discovery / Mastery / Secret), and locked secrets display "???" to create curiosity
- **Share cards**: Generate 600x315px trophy card images from any unlocked achievement. Share to clipboard, download as PNG, or post to X/Twitter with pre-filled text
- **Easter eggs**: Hidden achievements triggered by secret interactions (Konami code, typing "gg" in chat, Town Hall click combos, and more)
- **Persistence**: Achievements are saved server-side (`~/.agentcraft/achievements.json`) and survive across clients, browsers, and devices. Achievements unlocked on one client are synced to all connected clients via WebSocket

## Skill Scrolls

Collectible items scattered across the map:

- Walking near a scroll picks it up and shows its contents
- Each scroll represents a Claude Code skill/plugin that can be installed
- Install skills directly from the game UI

## Agent Teams

Heroes can be organized into **teams** (a lead agent plus teammates):

- Teams are configured via Claude Code's team configuration (`~/.claude/teams/`)
- Team members are grouped in the Agent Status Panel with shared status
- Team rings appear around grouped heroes in the 3D view and minimap
- Inbox messages visible in the side panel chat

## Remote Access

Share your AgentCraft instance with others via a secure tunnel link.

- **Access**: Open the Alliance Panel (top bar) and click "Open" on the Remote Access card
- **Secure link**: Generates a tunnel URL with token-based authentication — only people with the full link (including token) can connect
- **Configurable expiration**: Set how long the link stays active; a countdown timer is displayed in the Alliance Panel
- **Copy with one click**: Copy the share link directly from the Alliance Panel
- **Revoke instantly**: Click **Stop** to terminate the tunnel and revoke access immediately
- **Use cases**: Pair programming, demos, sharing progress with teammates, or connecting your own mobile device

## War Room (Alliance Hall)

Federate multiple AgentCraft instances into a shared battlefield. Each developer runs their own AgentCraft server — a Cloudflare Durable Object relay connects them so remote agents appear on every participant's map.

- **Create a room**: Open the Alliance Panel (top bar) and click "Create" on the War Room card. A room code is generated and a cloudflared tunnel starts automatically (~3-5 seconds)
- **Join a room**: Enter the room code in the "Join" tab. Your server connects to the same relay
- **Shared visibility**: Remote heroes appear as semi-transparent (70% opacity) on every participant's 3D map, with colored participant indicators
- **What's shared**: Hero state (active/idle/awaiting), missions (start/complete), file access activity (basename only for privacy), session roster, and notice board messages
- **What's NOT shared**: File contents, prompts, transcripts, or terminal access — coordination happens via the relay events + git + notice board
- **Participant list**: Each participant shows their display name (hostname), session count, and a deterministic color dot
- **Requirements**: `cloudflared` is required for NAT traversal. It is auto-installed if not found on your machine (via Homebrew on macOS, or direct binary download). No Cloudflare account needed — uses Quick Tunnels
- **Leave**: Click "Leave" to disconnect, stop the tunnel, and remove remote heroes from the map
- **Tunnel sharing**: War Room and Remote Access share the same cloudflared tunnel process (reference-counted). If both are active, the tunnel stays alive until both release it
- **Reconnection**: If the connection drops, the client automatically reconnects with exponential backoff (1s, 2s, 4s, ... max 30s)

## Mobile PWA

AgentCraft works as a **Progressive Web App** on mobile devices, providing a native-like experience.

- **Connect**: Scan the QR code shown in the Remote Access modal, or paste the share URL into your mobile browser
- **PWA Installation**: Add to your home screen for a fullscreen app experience:
  - iOS: Share button > "Add to Home Screen"
  - Android: Browser menu > "Install app"
- **Push Notifications**: Get notified when heroes need input (plan approvals, permission requests, questions) even when the app is closed. Requires PWA installation; iOS requires 16.4+
- **Mobile Setup Banner**: A dismissable onboarding banner prompts for PWA install and notification permissions on first use
- **Haptic Feedback**: Automatic vibration feedback — light taps for selections, medium for actions, heavy for destructive confirmations

## Active Loops

- **Press ?** to see all keyboard shortcuts anytime

## Troubleshooting

Common issues and fixes (see **references/troubleshooting.md** for the full list):

- **Heroes not appearing**: Ensure hooks are installed — run `npx @idosal/agentcraft install` and restart your agent sessions (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, or Cursor)
- **Heroes from other projects not appearing**: Open Settings → Game tab → disable "Filter to Current Project". The filter is ON by default and hides heroes/sessions that belong to other directories
- **Laggy/slow**: Enable Performance Mode in Settings; disable fog of war with **V**
- **Keyboard shortcuts not responding**: Ensure no input field is focused; click the 3D viewport first (non-Latin layouts are supported automatically)
- **Hero stuck in error/wrong state**: Dismiss the hero and restart its underlying agent session (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, or Cursor); or use Factory Reset
- **Approvals not appearing**: Re-install hooks, check permission mode is "Default", restart the session
- **Settings not persisting**: Check `~/.agentcraft/settings.json` is writable
- **Voice input not working**: Ensure your browser supports the Web Speech API (Chrome, Firefox, Edge). Check that microphone permissions are granted. iOS Safari has limited support
- **Mobile not connecting**: Verify Remote Access is active on the desktop. Check that the full URL (including the `?token=...` parameter) was copied. If the QR code won't scan, paste the URL manually
- **Remote access link expired**: Start a new Remote Access session from the Alliance Panel — links expire after the configured duration
- **LAN / reverse-proxy blank screen**: If localhost works but a LAN IP or custom hostname shows a blank screen, check DevTools for CORS-blocked asset requests. Forward `Host`/`X-Forwarded-Proto`, or set `AGENTCRAFT_TRUSTED_ORIGINS` and restart AgentCraft
- **Isolated agent not starting**: Ensure Docker Desktop is running (or Apple Containers on macOS 26+). Check disk space for image builds. On macOS, click "Always Allow" if prompted for Keychain access
- **War Room not connecting**: Ensure `cloudflared` is installed (it auto-installs, but check `which cloudflared`). Verify the room code is correct. Check that both machines can reach the relay (`curl -X POST https://agentcraft-warroom.workers.dev/rooms` should return a room code)
- **Remote heroes not appearing**: Check `GET /warroom/status` returns `active: true` on both machines. Remote sessions should appear in the session roster with `isRemote: true`. Try leaving and rejoining the room
- **Factory Reset**: Settings → About tab → **Reset All State** — clears all AgentCraft state without affecting your code or sessions. Or delete files manually under `~/.agentcraft/`

When an agent error occurs, **The Chronicler** (War Advisor) automatically pops up with a tip and a link to **getagentcraft.com/docs** for help. The Discord community is also available at **discord.gg/nEaZAH7C7F**.
